lines.text: A land named after a city of stone, taken by a company, freed after a long war, and tested ever since. This is the story of Zimbabwe.
Around the year 1100, the ancestors of the Shona began building Great Zimbabwe, a city of stone walls that grew rich on gold and cattle.
As Great Zimbabwe faded, the kingdom of Mutapa took over many of its lands, trading gold and ivory with the Portuguese.
In the nineteenth century, Lobengula ruled as king of the Ndebele. He would be their last.
Cecil Rhodes, a British mining magnate in southern Africa, wanted the land north of the Limpopo, and in time the country would bear his name.
In 1855 the explorer David Livingstone reached the great falls of the Zambezi, and named them after his queen, Victoria.
In 1890 Rhodes's company planted its flag where Harare, the capital, now stands.
Six years later the Ndebele and the Shona rose against the company's rule. The First Chimurenga was crushed, but never forgotten.
Joshua Nkomo would found ZAPU, and become one of the fathers of the country's independence.
Ian Smith, a farmer and former pilot, would lead the colony's white minority government, determined to keep power.
Robert Mugabe, a teacher turned nationalist, would lead the struggle for freedom, and then rule the new nation for thirty-seven years.
Emmerson Mnangagwa, long at Mugabe's side, would one day replace him.
In the fifties a great dam was built across the Zambezi at Kariba, creating one of the world's largest man-made lakes.
From 1964, guerrillas took up arms against white rule. The bush war would last fifteen years.
In 1965 the white government broke away from Britain and called the country Rhodesia. Almost no nation recognised it.
That break was the Unilateral Declaration of Independence, meant to keep power in the hands of the white minority.
In 1979, at Lancaster House in London, all sides agreed to end the war and hold free elections.
In 1980 the nation was born, Zimbabwe, named for the ancient city of stone.
Land became the great question. From 2000, white-owned farms were seized, and harvests collapsed.
Earlier, in the eighties, soldiers carried out massacres in Matabeleland, a wound still felt today.
Kirsty Coventry, born in Harare, would win seven Olympic medals in the pool, and in 2025 be elected head of the International Olympic Committee.
By 2008 prices were doubling in days. The Zimbabwe dollar became worthless, and people turned to foreign money.
In 2017 the army moved against Mugabe, and his long rule was over.
From the walls of Great Zimbabwe to today, its people are still shaping their nation's future.
